Subject: Morning Market Call - Thursday, September 6, 2001

Good morning,

After yesterday's trading, equities enter Thursday on unsteady ground. Another wave of earnings warnings weighed on tech names, and investors remain wary about where the economy is headed. Futures suggest a weak start.

On our radar today:

- Initial jobless claims, out at 8:30 a.m. A further increase would deepen worries about employment.
- Revisions to second-quarter productivity.
- Remarks from Fed officials in the wake of the Beige Book, which painted a picture of sluggish growth.
- Treasury yields, which have slipped as traders position for more rate cuts.

Ahead of Friday's payrolls release, we expect thin volume and headline-driven price action. Our advice is to be selective and watch risk closely.

We'll be back at midday.

Regards,
The Trading Desk

Subject: EBS concerns

Hi Marcus,

I'm writing about the EBS volumes on our production instances. While going through last month's AWS invoice, I spotted a few issues that I think we should examine before they grow into something worse.

To start, storage spending has gone up roughly 28% this quarter, while traffic has grown nowhere near that fast. Digging in, I found around forty volumes that aren't attached to any running instance. Several appear to be left over from the spring staging migration. Combined, they cost us a few hundred dollars each month, and no one appears to be responsible for them.

Next, a lot of our snapshots lack any retention policy. Some date back more than two years, and a number of them belong to volumes that have since been deleted. I can't tell whether we still need any of them for compliance or recovery, which is precisely why I want to check before anything gets removed.

Finally, I have some concerns about performance on the database volumes. A few of them are still running on gp2, and during last week's reporting jobs I noticed latency spikes that coincided with burst credits being exhausted. Switching to gp3 would likely solve this while also lowering costs, but I'd rather not do it without scheduling a maintenance window.

My proposal:

1. Give every volume an owner tag and a purpose tag, and mark anything without tags for review.
2. Create snapshot lifecycle policies that default to 30 to 90 days unless there's a reason for longer retention.
3. Schedule a gp2-to-gp3 migration for the database volumes, beginning with the least critical ones.

By the end of the week I can have a spreadsheet ready that lists the orphaned volumes and old snapshots. It would be a big help if you could review it and let me know which ones are safe to delete.

Are you free Thursday to go over this? Fifteen minutes should be plenty to settle on next steps.

Thanks,
Priya

Hot water become small and light, like smoke come off fire. Water rise. Up, up, up. Eyes not see it go. Water become air-water. Wise people call this "evaporate." Caveman call it water fly off.

Not only sea do this. Puddle do it. Wet rock do it. Mammoth fur wet after rain, sun dry it. Where wet go? Wet go up into sky. Plant leaves also let water go up. All wet things give small water to sky.

Now air-water is high. Up high, air is very cold. Brrr. Cold change air-water. Air-water squeeze close, like cavemen in cave when snow come. Many tiny water bits hold hands. Together they make cloud. Cloud white, cloud gray, cloud soft like fur. Wise people call this "condense." Caveman call it water gather and make cloud.

Cloud float along. Wind push cloud across hills, across trees, across caves. Cloud grow big. Cloud fill up fat with water. Cloud turn dark, turn heavy. Too heavy, cannot hold. **Abstract**

Because they combine strong perpendicular magnetic anisotropy with low saturation magnetization, tetragonal L1₀ Mn-Ga thin films have attracted significant attention for spintronics. Here we examine the effect of epitaxial strain on the magnetic behavior of ultrathin L1₀ Mn-Ga films deposited on single-crystal substrates. We grew films between a few and several tens of nanometers thick and characterized them using X-ray diffraction and magnetometry. As the films become thinner, the uniaxial anisotropy drops markedly, and this is accompanied by a measurable shift in the tetragonal distortion of the lattice. These observations suggest that, in the ultrathin limit, strain relaxation together with interfacial effects increasingly suppresses the anisotropy. Our results establish how far Mn-Ga can serve as a perpendicular magnetic layer at small thicknesses and offer guidance for designing thin-film devices.

# Navy Plans to Move 1,200 Sailors Across Three Carriers in One Deployment

NORFOLK, Va. — Roughly 1,200 sailors will serve on three separate aircraft carriers over the course of a single tour in an uncommon "three-hull swap," according to the Navy.

Under the plan, the crew members will transfer from ship to ship, and every one of the vessels bears the name of a U.S. president. The idea is to keep the sailors intact as a unit even as the ships they run are changed out around them.

The tour will kick off in Japan. From there, the sailors will travel around South America to Virginia, where they will assume control of a second carrier. Next, the crew will head west again toward the Pacific to arrive in San Diego, where the third ship is waiting.

Navy officials have characterized the swap as an efficient use of experienced personnel at a time when ships are shifting between homeports and maintenance schedules. Instead of breaking up a team and building a new one, the Navy holds a trained group of sailors together and moves the ships around them. This approach sidesteps the expense and upheaval of relocating an entire crew whenever a vessel changes location.

The sailors will face something quite different from an ordinary deployment. Usually, a sailor spends a tour on a single ship and gets to know its quirks, layout and routines. Here, they will have to adjust to three ships, each with its own peculiarities, even though the carriers have a shared design and mission.

The voyage around South America, spanning thousands of miles, is expected to be the toughest stretch of the swap. Carriers making that journey often serve as visible symbols of the Navy's global presence, and the transit will feature port calls and training en route.

The sailors' families will be affected as well, since the shifting locations could change where they can see their loved ones and how long the sailors spend away from home.

According to the Navy, the plan is part of a wider effort to manage an overstretched fleet and to give crews continuity while ships undergo repairs, upgrades and redeployment.

A wide range of add-ins can alter a loaf's taste, texture and appearance.

**Grains and seeds:** For crunch and extra nutrition, try sunflower, pumpkin, sesame, flax, poppy or chia seeds. Rolled oats, cracked wheat or cooked quinoa add substance.

**Flavor:** Rosemary, thyme, oregano and other herbs are good choices, as are roasted garlic, caramelized onion, cheese, olives and sun-dried tomatoes. For some heat, use black pepper or jalapeño.

**Sweet additions:** Breakfast loaves pair well with raisins, cranberries, chopped dates, walnuts, cinnamon, honey or molasses.

**Texture and richness:** Adding milk, butter, olive oil, an egg or yogurt gives a softer crumb. Potato flakes or mashed potato help the bread stay moist.

**Other flours:** Rye, whole wheat or spelt flour brings depth, while a spoonful of malt powder helps the crust brown.

To spread dry add-ins evenly, fold them in toward the end of kneading.

The first bullet hit Daniel Whitmore in the chest while the vault door was still swinging open.

Getting shot had not been part of his plan. Truthfully, robbing a bank had not been part of his plan either, not until three weeks before, when a foreclosure notice showed up and a medical bill swallowed what remained of his savings. The scheme was straightforward: a mask, a duffel bag, a secondhand pistol that looked almost like a toy, and ten minutes of nerve.

Ortiz, the heavyset security guard, squeezed off two more shots. Each one landed on Daniel like a hard shove, the kind you get in a packed hallway. He stumbled backward into a marble pillar. Then he glanced down.

His jacket had three holes in it. He was not bleeding.

"Stay down!" Ortiz yelled, his voice breaking. He fired once more. The bullet flattened on Daniel's shoulder and fell to the floor with a faint metallic clink.

For a moment the lobby went completely quiet. The tellers, the customers sprawled on the tile, the guard holding his smoking revolver: everyone was staring at Daniel, and he was staring right back.

"I believe," he said carefully, "that this is not going the way it is supposed to."

Ortiz let his gun sink. His hands shook. "What are you?"

"I have no idea," Daniel confessed. He pulled off the mask, since there seemed little point in hiding anymore. "Believe me, I am just as surprised as you are."

Sirens sounded in the distance, drawing closer. Daniel weighed his situation with the composure of someone who had just learned the rules were different now. He could run off with the cash. He could probably stroll straight through a police line without a scratch. But when he looked at the scared faces on the floor, the duffel bag suddenly made him feel ashamed.

He placed it on the counter, open and empty.

"I am sorry for the disturbance," he told the closest teller, a young woman gripping her badge. "I came here to take money. I am not going to."

Outside, the police had gathered in large numbers. Daniel walked out into the sunlight with his hands up. Officers yelled. Shots were fired one after another, and every bullet hit him and dropped away without effect. He waited patiently for them to finish.

"Gentlemen," he said, "I am ready to be arrested. My only request is that someone tell me why I cannot be hurt, because I would really like to understand it."

Silence fell. Then the officer in charge, pale and uncertain, gradually lowered his weapon.

It occurred to Daniel that invincibility did not fix his problems. The foreclosure notice was still sitting at home. The medical bill was no smaller. Yet something was different. For the first time in months he felt no fear, and he had a feeling this would prove more important than all the money in the vault.

He extended his wrists. "Please," he said. "Let's get started."

Autorotation is the technique a helicopter pilot uses to land safely when the engine fails or the tail rotor quits. Rather than being powered by the engine, the main rotor keeps turning because the helicopter is descending and air flows upward through it. The pilot then draws on the energy stored in the spinning rotor to soften the touchdown.

It works much like a maple seed twirling as it drops. During normal flight, air is drawn downward through the rotor disc. In autorotation, the descent sends air upward through the disc, which turns the blades. Rotor speed (RPM) must stay within safe limits: too low and the blades lose lift, too high and the structure could be damaged.

**Steps in a typical autorotation**

1. **Recognize the failure.** Signs include a warning horn or light, a change in engine sound, or the nose yawing as torque is lost. Recognizing it quickly is essential.

2. **Lower the collective immediately.** Doing so decreases the pitch of the main rotor blades, cutting drag and allowing the rotor to keep turning. This must happen within a second or two, since rotor speed starts dropping at once.

3. **Maintain rotor RPM.** Watching the tachometer, the pilot adjusts the collective to hold RPM in the green arc.

4. **Establish the glide.** With the cyclic, the pilot sets the best glide speed, which varies by aircraft and is often about 60 to 80 knots. Airspeed and rotor RPM are the two key things to control.

5. **Choose a landing area.** The pilot selects an appropriate spot, preferably facing into the wind and free of obstacles, and heads for it, using the pedals to keep the helicopter in trim.

6. **Make a radio call and prepare for landing.** Time permitting, the pilot declares an emergency and quickly checks for what caused the failure, for example by trying to restart the engine.

7. **Flare.** About 40 to 100 feet above the ground, the pilot brings the cyclic back to lift the nose. This reduces both forward speed and descent rate while also raising rotor RPM.

8. **Level the aircraft.** Right before touchdown, the pilot uses the cyclic to level the helicopter so it lands on its skids or wheels.

9. **Cushion the landing.** Close to the ground, the pilot raises the collective to spend the rotor's remaining energy, slowing the descent and making the touchdown gentler.

10. **Land and lower the collective.** Once down, the pilot holds the cyclic neutral, fully lowers the collective, and brings the helicopter to a stop.

Pilots rehearse autorotations frequently during training, often ending in a power recovery, so that the maneuver becomes second nature.

Because mesons carrying spin-exotic quantum numbers such as J^PC = 1^−+ cannot arise from a quark-antiquark pair alone, they are considered unambiguous signs of hybrid mesons or multiquark states. At CERN, the COMPASS experiment looks for these states in the diffractive dissociation of a 190 GeV/c negative pion beam on a proton target, exploiting the wide acceptance of its two-stage magnetic spectrometer. Here we report new partial-wave analysis results for the π−π−π+, ηπ− and η′π− final states, all extracted from one data sample. Each of these channels shows significant intensity in the spin-exotic 1^−+ wave. We investigate whether the signal is resonant by fitting the mass dependence of the partial-wave amplitudes, including their phase motion with respect to well-established resonances. The π1(1600) parameters obtained are compared among the decay modes, and we discuss the contribution of non-resonant processes to the 1^−+ wave.

Single-use plastics show up everywhere in everyday life. Plastic bags, straws, bottles and utensils are used for a few minutes and then tossed out. Yet these things do not simply vanish. In my opinion, governments should prohibit single-use plastic products, since the damage they do is far greater than the convenience they offer.

The first argument concerns harm to the environment. Plastic needs hundreds of years to decompose, and in the meantime it collects in oceans, rivers and landfills. Sea turtles confuse plastic bags with jellyfish, and seabirds give bits of plastic to their chicks as food. Eventually plastic fragments into tiny microplastics, which have now turned up in drinking water, in food and even in human blood. This endangers both animals and people.

The second argument is that recycling by itself falls short. Many people think tossing plastic into a recycling bin takes care of the issue, but only around nine percent of all plastic ever produced has actually been recycled. When the system itself is broken, governments cannot rely on individuals to solve the problem. A ban sends an unmistakable signal and pushes companies toward better alternatives.

Some argue that a ban would increase costs for businesses and shoppers. That is a reasonable worry. Still, a number of countries have already put bans in place and handled the transition well. Reusable bags, paper straws and refillable containers are now widespread, and they frequently get cheaper as more people adopt them.

To conclude, a ban on single-use plastics is both sensible and needed. It safeguards the environment, spurs innovation, and demonstrates that society takes seriously its duty to future generations.

**Prompt: "What would the world be like if the Allies had won the war?"**

---

By the time Karl Reinhardt had finished reading the thread aloud, it had four thousand upvotes. His grandfather listened from the corner of the Bremen apartment, a blanket across his knees and his eyes shut.

"Read me the top comment again," the old man said.

Karl cleared his throat. "'Picture a Germany torn to pieces, occupied, and forced to pay. Picture a Europe split between rival powers, with armies lining every border. Picture the Reich in ruins, with no Führer to lead it.' Opa, it's only a writing prompt. Everybody knows it's made up."

"Do they?"

"Of course. The Allies lost. We won. The Reich is strong. Just look around."

His grandfather opened his eyes. They were watery and pale, but steady. "I'm ninety-one, Karl. I have been looking around for a very long time."

Karl almost laughed, but the expression on the old man's face stopped him. Outside, the evening broadcast was beginning. The familiar anthem came through the thin walls, the same one that had opened every evening Karl could remember.

"In the story," Karl said slowly, "people say the world would be free. That you could say whatever you wanted. That nobody would vanish in the night." He shrugged. "No one believes that. No one could."

"I had a brother," his grandfather said. "Matthias. In 1943 he said something in a bakery, and by the next morning he was gone. Your grandmother told me not to go looking for him. So I didn't." He stopped for a moment. "I have never forgiven myself for doing as I was told."

The room fell silent. The anthem rose through the wall.

"You want to know what that world would be like?" the old man asked. "I think it would be a world where you could ask me that question without dropping your voice."

Karl realized he had been whispering the whole time.

He looked at the screen, at thousands of strangers picturing a world where they weren't afraid, and felt something he couldn't name, something that had been trained out of him before he could even walk.

"Write something," his grandfather said. "Beneath their story. Only one line."

"They'd trace it."

"Probably."

Karl's fingers hung above the keyboard. On the street below, a patrol car drifted by, slow and in no hurry. He thought about Matthias, the bakery, the sound of a door shutting.

Then, with care, he typed: *I think I'd have liked living there.*

He didn't hit send. Not yet. But for the first time in his life, he let the words stay on the screen, and he didn't erase them.

What counts as cute is a matter of opinion, but certain animals reliably rank near the top.

**Young animals of almost any kind** usually come out ahead because of their large eyes, rounded faces and awkward movements. Puppies, kittens and ducklings are all good examples.

Several wild species are especially popular:

- **Red pandas** sport fluffy reddish-brown fur, a ringed tail and a round face with a mask-like pattern.
- **Sea otters** hold hands while sleeping to avoid drifting apart, and they float on their backs cracking shells open on their bellies.
- **Quokkas**, little marsupials native to Western Australia, look as if they are always smiling.
- **Baby elephants** totter about on sturdy legs and stumble over their own trunks.
- **Fennec foxes** combine huge ears with very small bodies.
- **Pygmy hedgehogs** roll up into prickly balls small enough to sit in your hand.
- **Axolotls** have a loyal fan base thanks to their feathery gills and constant grin.
- **Penguin chicks** waddle clumsily in coats of fluffy gray down.

Scientists call the response these creatures provoke the "baby schema" effect, which explains how features such as large eyes and round heads set off our instinct to nurture.

Here are five ideas for using up a ripe avocado.

1. **Classic guacamole.** Mash it together with lime juice, salt, diced red onion, cilantro and a bit of chopped jalapeno. Leave a few chunks for texture.

2. **Avocado toast.** Spread the avocado over a thick slice of crusty toast, then top it with flaky salt, chili flakes and a squeeze of lemon. Add a fried or poached egg to make it a complete meal.

3. **Creamy smoothie.** Put half an avocado in the blender with a banana, spinach, your preferred milk and a touch of honey. You get a silky texture without much avocado flavor.

4. **Chocolate mousse.** Blend the avocado with cocoa powder, maple syrup, a little milk and a pinch of salt until it is perfectly smooth, then refrigerate it for an hour. The result is rich and unexpectedly indulgent.

5. **Stuffed avocado.** Cut it in half, take out the pit and fill the cavity with tuna salad, chicken salad or a combination of tomato, corn and black beans. Spoon it right out of the skin.

**Abstract**

We describe adaptive mesh refinement (AMR) simulations of the cosmological light cone aimed at generating synthetic survey data for the Sunyaev-Zel'dovich effect (SZE). With an adaptively refined hydrodynamic code, we track galaxy cluster formation within a large cosmological volume, and we build a light cone by stacking simulation outputs and projecting them along the line of sight. The thermal SZE signal of each cluster is calculated from gas properties such as density and temperature. From this we produce mock SZE maps, cluster catalogs, and number counts as functions of redshift and signal strength. These synthetic surveys make it possible to test strategies for finding clusters, to quantify selection effects that matter for present and future millimeter-wave experiments, and to evaluate how strongly cluster counts depend on the underlying cosmological parameters.

# Palmer Says He Gets Why Woods Is Skipping Bay Hill

**ORLANDO, Fla.** — Arnold Palmer says he bears no grudge against Tiger Woods, the most famous golfer in the world, for passing on the tournament that is named after Palmer.

This week, the 85-year-old king of golf, who hosts the Arnold Palmer Invitational, said he understands why Woods chose not to play at Bay Hill. Woods has been a regular at the event for much of his career and has won it more often than anyone else, but his game has been falling apart and he is trying to be careful about how he spends his time.

"I know what he's going through," Palmer said. "A player has to do what he thinks is best for his game, and I respect that. I'd love to have him here, and the fans would too, but I understand."

Woods is fighting to get ready for the Masters at Augusta National next month, a tournament where he has collected four green jackets. For weeks, his preparation has been overshadowed by doubts about whether he can sharpen his game in time. In recent outings he has sprayed tee shots, looked unsure around the greens and shown a visible lack of rhythm, far from the commanding form that earned him 14 major titles.

Time is not on Woods' side. With the Masters just weeks off, every day spent away from competition is a calculated gamble. Skipping events ahead of a major costs a player the chance to work through problems under pressure, yet Woods and his team seem to have concluded that practicing at home, out of view of the cameras and the scorecards, is the wiser path.

Palmer, who has had a close relationship with Woods for years and has frequently given him advice, said he was not concerned that the younger player would dwell on the choice.

"He's a competitor. He's going to figure out how to get ready," Palmer said. "He always has."

Orlando will notice his absence. Woods ranks among golf's biggest attractions, and his appearances at Bay Hill have long meant larger crowds, stronger TV ratings and added excitement around the grounds. Tournament officials had hoped he would at least come look at the course before heading to Augusta, but they have said they respect that the call is his to make.

The response is characteristic of Palmer, who has spent decades treating fellow golfers generously. He has mentored several generations of players and has often said the game is greater than any single tournament or any single name.

Even so, he made it plain that he wants to see Woods back in action soon, and playing better.

"The Masters is a special place for him, and for all of us," Palmer said. "I hope he gets it going. Golf needs Tiger playing well."

For the moment, attention moves to the rest of the Bay Hill field, where contenders will chase a win in Palmer's honor. Woods, for his part, will keep preparing privately with a single aim: showing up at Augusta ready to compete.

Whether the effort pays off is yet to be determined. What is certain is that the golf world will be paying close attention, and that the game's elder statesman is firmly on his side.

Few ethical issues in modern science are as contested as the use of animals in research. Supporters point out that animal studies have helped produce major medical breakthroughs, such as vaccines, insulin and organ transplants. Without this work, many diseases we can now treat might still be deadly. Researchers contend that limited animal testing is justified when the aim is to save human lives.

Opponents note that animals can feel pain and fear, and they argue that making animals suffer for human benefit is hard to defend morally. In addition, results from animal models do not always carry over to humans, which undercuts some of the claimed benefits.

I believe animal research can be ethical only when strict conditions are met. It should be used only when there is no alternative, limited to the smallest necessary scale, and designed to minimize suffering. The "three Rs" of replacement, reduction and refinement provide a practical framework. As technologies like organ-on-a-chip systems and computer modeling advance, we should aim for a future in which animal testing is uncommon. In the meantime, careful regulation and openness are crucial.

Because our sense of taste developed in a world where calories were hard to come by. Fat, sugar and salt were scarce and precious, so people evolved powerful cravings for them, and the brain releases dopamine as a reward when we eat them. Today's food companies take advantage of this by designing products with exactly the right balance of these ingredients, frequently at low cost and in enormous volumes. Healthy foods such as vegetables tend to have fewer calories and less intense flavor, so they deliver a weaker reward. Our judgment is also skewed: many of the "tastiest" foods are treats eaten for enjoyment rather than nourishment, which makes their drawbacks more noticeable. Lots of delicious foods, including ripe fruit, grilled fish and fresh bread with olive oil, are entirely healthy.

Since the atmosphere turns together with the planet, Earth's rotation has no meaningful direct effect on how long a flight takes. A plane travels relative to the surrounding air rather than the ground beneath it. As a result, an aircraft neither gains nor loses time just because the surface is rotating under it.

Rotation does, however, affect travel times indirectly through wind patterns. The prevailing westerlies, the jet stream among them, are partly a product of Earth's rotation. Eastbound flights, like New York to London, frequently get a boost from tailwinds and arrive earlier, whereas westbound flights fight headwinds and take more time. Rotation also produces small effects like the Coriolis force, but navigation already accounts for these, and their impact on duration is negligible.

**"American Pie" Lyrics in McLean's Hand Fetch $1.2 Million at Auction**

NEW YORK -- Don McLean's original handwritten lyrics for "American Pie" have been sold at auction for $1.2 million, a figure that highlights the lasting appeal of one of American music's most famous songs.

Containing drafts, notes and revisions, the manuscript provides an uncommon glimpse into how the singer-songwriter crafted the eight-and-a-half-minute ballad. Released in 1971, the song hit No. 1 in 1972 and is still McLean's biggest hit.

Not many pop songs have sparked so much argument. The verses are packed with symbols, from a jester and a king to a "day the music died," generally taken as a reference to the 1959 plane crash that took the lives of Buddy Holly, Ritchie Valens and J.P. "The Big Bopper" Richardson. Fans and critics have spent decades debating what the rest of the imagery means.

McLean has long refused to explain the song in full. He has said, though, that anyone who carefully studies the lyrics and notes up for sale will discover what the song means.

"Basically, they will see what it's about," he has said of the material, while still declining to spell it out himself.

According to auction officials, the lot drew strong interest, with multiple bidders vying for the manuscript. They called it an important piece of musical and cultural history, given how popular the song has been across generations and its place in the nation's memory.

Scholars of popular music say the sale points to an expanding market for items connected to famous songwriters. Handwritten lyric sheets, they observe, can reveal a creative process that finished recordings hide, including lines that were struck out, reworked or dropped.

The buyer's identity was not revealed. It remains unclear whether the new owner will make the manuscript available to the public or help resolve the long-standing mystery of what the song means.

Applying for a job before typewriters spread in the late nineteenth century was very different from the process we know now. No standard résumé existed, and hiring relied largely on personal ties, reputation and handwritten correspondence.

## How people heard about openings

**Word of mouth and social networks.** The majority of positions were filled through relatives, neighbors, fellow churchgoers and tradespeople. A friend might tell a farmer that a blacksmith was looking for a helper, or a merchant might ask his family whether they knew a capable clerk. Reputation was hugely important, since in small communities everyone's character and work habits were common knowledge.

**Apprenticeships and guilds.** The standard path into a skilled trade was an apprenticeship. Parents or guardians frequently arranged a place directly with a master craftsman, sometimes for a fee. In European towns, guilds controlled entry into a trade, so learning about openings depended on having ties to the guild system.

**Public notices.** Employers in towns and cities put up handbills or notices on doors, in marketplaces and at inns. Newspapers, which became widespread in the 1700s, printed advertisements; colonial American papers, for instance, published notices looking for servants, tutors, clerks and laborers. At hiring fairs, held in parts of England and elsewhere, workers and employers could meet in a public setting. Laborers stood in the town square, sometimes holding a tool or emblem of their trade, to show what kind of work they could do.

## How people applied

**Letters of introduction and recommendation.** Applicants for clerical, professional or household positions often depended on a recommendation letter from someone respected, such as a minister, a former employer or a local official. Such a letter worked much like a modern reference and could carry more weight than anything the applicant said personally.

**Handwritten letters of application.** Educated candidates wrote by hand, usually in a formal, courteous tone, outlining their qualifications and requesting consideration. Handwriting mattered: a clerk's position hinged on neat, readable penmanship, so the letter doubled as a sample of the applicant's work.

**In-person visits.** In many trades and manual jobs, applying just meant turning up. Someone would visit a workshop, farm or shop, talk with the owner and possibly show their skills right there.

## Why it worked this way

In the absence of mass communication, and with literacy limited in many regions, trust served as the main currency. Employers wanted people someone could vouch for, so patronage and personal connections counted for more than formal qualifications. Written records did exist, but they reinforced relationships rather than taking their place.

For your assignment, you might compare this with today's hiring, where résumés and online job postings are the norm, to show how technology transformed the process.
